tldr: Headlines across 20 buckets converge on a cascading death-toll and tunnel-rescue narrative for the Nepal-Tibet glacial flood (toll past 1,000; hundreds of hydropower workers feared trapped in mud-filled tunnels). A secondary thread in US and German headlines foregrounds China's suppression of Tibet flood footage, while a climate-justice argument — that Nepal bears disproportionate costs for emissions it did not produce — surfaces only in opinion-outlet and Vietnamese headlines.

single_outlet_findings.finding: Headline 'The Floods Nepal Didn't Cause' encodes the climate-justice moral argument entirely in the title — the only headline in the corpus that assigns implicit causal blame to high-emitting nations without naming them.

Leads its first headline with China's censorship rather than the humanitarian toll, making state suppression the primary story — the starkest editorial contrast to all other US outlets' death-toll or rescue framing.

Only headline in the corpus to scrutinise Nepal's own institutional response ('hesitance to accept foreign help'), an accountability angle absent from every other outlet including those in the region.
Headline frames the event as a systemic warning-system failure ('struck without warning') rather than a casualty scorecard — the only explanatory-causal headline among all US outlets.
Only headline in the entire corpus to foreground a heroism/human-interest narrative (principal saving 900 students) rather than death counts, missing tallies, or rescue operations.

bottom_line: The headline layer is a near-global death-toll scoreboard and tunnel-rescue race; China's information crackdown in Tibet appears in only two Western outlets' titles, and climate justice is confined entirely to opinion-magazine and Vietnamese headlines.
